Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

vignette: At twenty-two, Mateo Rivera was still trying to live inside his body after the ceasefire in his hometown fractured overnight. He had been delivering supply crates through the eastern market when a mortar landed without warning, the violent crack of concrete and the sudden, desperate sprint of a crowd tearing around him. Pinned beneath a collapsed awning, he lay trapped in a knot of dust and shouting feet. When he finally scrambled free, the relief of survival calcified into a permanent state of waiting for the next strike. His shoulders stopped relaxing. His eyes never stopped scanning. In the months that followed, returning to his American university life, quiet spaces felt more dangerous than loud ones. He stood with his back to the wall, his neck perpetually tight, his breathing shallow and rapid, as if his ribs were a caged thing bracing for impact. Now working as a product manager, his open-plan office became a daily rehearsal for the market’s violence. Glass partitions and constantly rotating visitors stripped away any sense of perimeter. A colleague leaning too quickly over his desk to hand over a file would make Mateo’s entire frame jerk, his pulse hammering as if a threat had breached his station. He had come to believe the office was only one unexpected shift away from catastrophe. His nervous system refused to log him as safe. Every phone notification triggered a flinch that left his hands trembling for minutes. He stopped wearing headphones, convinced that relying on digital cues would leave him blind to approaching danger. His body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, a low-grade current that never broke and turned routine stand-up meetings into exercises in controlled panic. He remained superalert or watchful or on guard, never allowing his attention to settle. The relentless pressure of his own vigilance eventually became unbearable, and that unrelenting threat state directly drove him toward maladaptive strategies. Mateo found that the only way to interrupt the crushing tightness in his chest was to ground himself in sharper pain. During late nights at his kitchen counter, he would press a paperclip into the pad of his thumb until the burn cut through the fog, deliberately hurting myself physically to release overwhelming feelings that pooled in his ribs. As the sting faded, he would immediately turn to his phone, refreshing group chats and sending voice notes to his sister, explaining that he kept asking others to reassure me that I am okay, needing the repetition of safety to quiet his racing thoughts. He also began methodically patting down his arms and legs every time he moved between rooms, constantly checking body for signs of danger or injury, as if confirming the absence of wounds would convince his system it was no longer in the zone. These attempts to manage the distress only fed the very alarm he was trying to quiet. Every time Mateo checked his body, his hands lingered on his pulse points, his breath catching at the slightest flutter, convincing him that the panic itself was evidence of an ongoing wound. The reassurance he sought was temporary; once his sister stopped answering or the comfort wore off, the silence felt heavier, and his guard snapped back up, more tightly than before. The physical release of pain did not reset his system; it only left him exhausted and hyper-focused on the aftershocks. Consequently, the constant checking and the desperate need for external validation became anchors, pulling his threat perception back to red alert with every cycle. He was certain that if he stopped monitoring his surroundings or stopped seeking confirmation from others, the collapse would happen again without warning. By the time he scheduled his first appointment, Mateo had stopped taking the lead on his team’s sprint reviews, defaulting to email to avoid face-to-face scrutiny. His product launches were slipping, not from a lack of competence, but from a paralysis that set in whenever the office hummed with too many conversations. He sat on the edge of his therapist’s chair, hands pressed flat against his knees, shoulders hunched as if bracing for an impact that never came. He wanted to understand how to let his shoulders drop, how to sit in a room without counting the exits or flinching at the rustle of a file folder. What frightened him most was that the calm he craved might simply be the quiet before another collapse, but he had exhausted every other way to keep himself from breaking. He hoped someone could help him untangle the wire so he could finally stand still without feeling like he was falling apart.
